title: Integrated Security & Compliance Controlbook: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence & Exceptions
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s operational controls and procedures across RBAC & authentication, audit logging, data residency & retention, Secure SDLC requirements, incident-response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and the risk & exceptions process. It is intended for engineering, security, and compliance stakeholders and serves as the single-source controlbook for audit preparation and operational decisions.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: All Redwood-hosted and customer-facing control plane services, private deployment control planes, and telemetry pipelines used for security/compliance evidence. Excludes product feature design docs and individual team onboarding notes.
- Audience: Security, infra, eng-sre, eng-platform, product, legal, and compliance owners.

1) Principles and High-level requirements
- Least privilege: Every identity (human or machine) must have the minimum privileges required for business function.
- Separation of duties: Sensitive operations must require multi-person approval or RBAC-enforced separation where feasible.
- Defend-in-depth: Controls are layered (network, identity, platform, monitoring, audit).
- Evidence-first: All controls must produce tamper-evident evidence suitable for audit (time-stamped logs, immutable storage).

2) RBAC & Authentication (Operational standard)
- Identity providers: Primary SSO is Okta. Service identities must use short-lived certificates or OIDC tokens issued by internal token service with machine identity rotation.
- Role model:
  - Roles: admin, infra-operator, sre-oncall, platform-deployer, security-auditor, read-only-analytics, customer-support-limited.
  - Principle: Role naming is authoritative in the org directory; teams may create team-scoped roles but must map to canonical roles for org-wide reporting.
- Groups and policy management:
  - Groups are created in Okta and mapped to platform RBAC via SCIM where supported.
  - Policy changes (create/update/delete) require a PR in infra-iam repo and must be approved by the security team and owning service team. Changes are recorded in Git with signed commits.
- Privilege elevation and just-in-time access:
  - Access to high-risk roles uses ephemeral elevation (max 8-hour session) and requires justification via the access request system. All elevation requests create a ticket and are logged.
- Periodic review:
  - Quarterly access review: service owners run org-access reports and reconcile membership. Evidence artifacts (review outputs) are stored in audit-bucket/enforcements/YYYY-MM.
- Service accounts and secrets:
  - No long-lived static keys in code. All secrets must be in Vault (KMS-backed) and provisioned using the secrets broker with explicit ACLs.

3) Audit logging (what, where, retention)
- Logging scope:
  - Identity events: SSO logins, token creations, role elevations, group changes.
  - Control plane actions: deploys, config changes, rollout events, policy updates.
  - Data access events: access to customer data stores, key operations (encrypt/decrypt), KMS usage.
  - Infra events: node provisioning, autoscaler decisions, capacity changes.
- Immutable log pipeline:
  - All logs are forwarded to the centralized logging pipeline (platform-logs) and written to append-only storage (WORM) with write-once/backups.
  - System-of-record for audit evidence is audit-archives (S3 with object-lock enabled).
- Retention and tiers:
  - Critical security logs: 7 years (legal & compliance).
  - Operational logs (high-fidelity traces): 90 days hot, 2 years cold (compressed).
  - Analytics logs: 1 year.
- Access to logs:
  - Access is RBAC controlled; security-auditor and designated incident responders have read access. Log exports require a logged request and approval for forensic copies.
- Alerting and integrity:
  - Integrity checks (checksums + periodic attestations) run weekly. Alerts on ingestion gaps, tampering incidents, or retention policy violations route to oncall + security.

4) Data residency & retention policies
- Regional controls:
  - Customer data must remain within the customer-approved region(s). For hosted customers, data-at-rest and backups are pinned to region(s) in customer contract.
  - Cross-region replication is disabled by default; enabled only with documented approvals and compensating controls (encryption, contractual consent).
- Data classification and retention matrix (summary):
  - PII / Customer Data: retention per contract (typical default: 7 years for backups, active retention configurable per-customer).
  - Logs & telemetry: see Audit Logging section.
  - Operational artifacts (build artifacts, images): 90 days by default unless required for investigations.
- Data deletion and proof of deletion:
  - Deletion requests use documented workflows; proof-of-deletion artifacts (object tombstone, deletion-job id, KMS ledger entry) are archived to evidence storage.
  - For hard-deletion, process includes key destruction and verification steps; legal/custodian approvals are required for regulated datasets.

5) Secure SDLC standards (developer & CI/CD requirements)
- Requirements for every repo that touches customer or security-sensitive code/data:
  1. Enforce branch protection: admin-approved PRs only, required code owners.
  2. Static analysis: SAST scan on PRs (fail-build on high-severity findings), dependency scanning automatically on push.
  3. Secret scanning: prevent commits with secrets; all secrets must be provisioned via Vault.
  4. Container image provenance: images must be built in ephemeral CI runners, signed, and stored in signed registries.
  5. SRE/Platform gating: Deploy pipelines must verify deploy-time policy (region, role, canary configs).
- Release & rollout controls:
  - Canary first: automated canary deployment of at least 5% traffic for 30 minutes with health checks and rollback gates.
  - Security review: any change affecting auth, RBAC, or data handling requires security sign-off prior to production rollout.

6) Incident response — security procedures and evidence preservation
- Roles and responsibilities:
  - Incident Commander (IC): coordinates cross-team response.
  - Security Lead: leads technical investigation.
  - Forensics SME: responsible for evidence collection and chain-of-custody.
  - Communications: owns internal/external notifications and legal escalation.
- Triage & containment checklist (high level):
  1. Triage severity (P0–P3) per incident taxonomy and notify IC.
  2. Isolate affected systems (network ACLs, revoke ephemeral credentials, freeze deploys).
  3. Preserve evidence (start legal-forensics runbook: snapshot VMs, copy logs to WORM archive, capture process memory where safe).
  4. Perform root-cause analysis and mitigation steps with documented timeline.
  5. Post-incident review and update controls.
- Evidence handling:
  - Chain-of-custody: every evidence transfer is logged with actor, timestamp, and purpose.
  - Forensic snapshots are stored in a dedicated evidence-bucket with restricted ACLs and object-lock for the duration required by the investigation.
- Notification and legal requirements:
  - If customer data is implicated, follow the customer-notification checklist in the incident playbook and coordinate with legal and customer-success.
  - Regulatory (e.g., GDPR breach): timeline-driven notifications (72-hours to regulator) with evidence package prepared by security + legal.

7) Compliance evidence workflows (audit readiness)
- Evidence catalog and owners:
  - Each control (RBAC, logging, retention, SDLC) has a designated evidence owner responsible for maintaining artifacts and responding to auditor requests.
  - Evidence types: access review exports, signed IAM policy commits, immutable logs, retention configuration snapshots, build/signing logs, vulnerability scan results, incident timelines.
- Automation and periodic attestations:
  - Automations generate monthly attestations: access-review snapshots, logging-integrity attestations, and retention-policy snapshots. These are stored in evidence-archive/YYYY-MM and pushed to the compliance dashboard.
- Audit request process:
  1. Auditor submits request via compliance-requests service.
  2. Evidence owner acknowledges within 3 business days and provides initial artifacts within 10 business days (or negotiates scope).
  3. All delivered artifacts are recorded with delivery hash and stored in the audit-archives bucket.

8) Risk acceptance and exceptions process
- Risk exceptions are temporary (max 90 days) and require: rationale, compensating controls, test plan, and owner.
- Approval workflow:
  1. Submit exception request in exceptions-tracker (description, affected controls, risk level).
  2. Security reviews and assigns risk-rating; high-risk exceptions escalate to CISO and legal.
  3. Approvals recorded with expiry date and mitigation steps.
  4. Automatic reminders at 30/7 days before expiry; renewal requires full justification and re-approval.
- Compensating controls examples:
  - Network micro-segmentation, additional monitoring/alerting, temporary reduction of privileges, mandatory MFA for all affected accounts.

9) Operational responsibilities and ownership
- Security team: policy design, reviews, evidence custody for org-level controls, incident leadership.
- Eng-sre: logging pipeline, SLOs for evidence ingestion, forensics tooling support.
- Eng-platform / infra: enforce RBAC in platform, CI/CD gating, secrets broker.
- Service owners: maintain service-specific RBAC configs, run quarterly access reviews, preserve per-service artifacts.

10) Reporting, metrics, and SLOs for controls
- Key metrics:
  - Access-review completion rate (target 100% quarterly).
  - Time-to-evidence for audit requests (target median <= 5 business days).
  - Log ingestion SLO (99.9% within 2 minutes of generation).
  - Number of open risk exceptions (target 0–2 low-risk, 0 high-risk).
- Regular reporting cadence: monthly security dashboard, quarterly compliance readiness report for executive leadership.

Appendices and references:
- Appendix A: Sample RBAC policy snippet (YAML) and PR template description.
- Appendix B: Incident evidence checklist and forensic runbook (links to runbooks).
- Appendix C: Retention configuration table and sample KMS ledger entry.
- References: platform-logs runbook, infra-iam repo, exceptions-tracker guide, legal data-privacy playbook.

Maintenance and review:
- This document is reviewed annually by the Security team and immediately after any major regulatory or architectural change. Change proposals must be submitted as PRs against the controlbook repo with at least one security reviewer.

Contact and escalation:
- For questions or approvals: security@redwood-inference.example / #security channel.
- Emergency incident pager: security-oncall (see eng-sre oncall roster).
